title: Ibrance (palbociclib): Mechanism, Approved Use, Dosing/Administration, Monitoring, Safety, and Clinical Evidence for MSL/HCP Reference
summary: Ibrance (palbociclib) is an oral cyclin-dependent kinase 4/6 (CDK4/6) inhibitor marketed by Pfizer, approved for HR-positive, HER2-negative advanced/metastatic breast cancer in combination with an aromatase inhibitor, fulvestrant, or (as of 2024) inavolisib plus fulvestrant, and most recently (June 2026) with trastuzumab ± pertuzumab and endocrine therapy for HR+/HER2+ maintenance therapy. Core prescribing information centers on a 125 mg once-daily oral dose for 21 days followed by 7 days off (28-day cycle), taken with food, with mandatory neutropenia monitoring (CBC at baseline, each cycle start, and Day 15 of cycles 1–2) and boxed/label warnings for neutropenia, ILD/pneumonitis, and embryo-fetal toxicity. Pivotal trials PALOMA-1/2/3 established consistent, large progression-free survival benefit when palbociclib was added to endocrine therapy, though none of the studies showed a statistically significant overall survival benefit versus endocrine therapy alone.

claims.text: Ibrance (palbociclib) capsules/tablets are indicated for the treatment of adult patients with hormone receptor-positive (HR+), HER2-negative advanced or metastatic breast cancer in combination with an aromatase inhibitor as initial endocrine-based therapy, or with fulvestrant in patients with disease progression following endocrine therapy.

claims.text: In the PATINA trial, patients were randomized 1:1 to receive palbociclib with trastuzumab (±pertuzumab) and endocrine therapy (fulvestrant or an aromatase inhibitor: anastrozole, letrozole, or exemestane), or trastuzumab (±pertuzumab) and endocrine therapy alone, after induction with a taxane and trastuzumab (±pertuzumab); the trial met its primary PFS endpoint with an investigator-assessed hazard ratio of 0.76 (95% CI 0.59–0.97).

claims.text: Based on findings from animal studies and its mechanism of action, IBRANCE can cause fetal harm when administered to a pregnant woman; animal reproduction studies showed embryo-fetal toxicity at maternal exposures ≥4 times human clinical exposure (AUC). Females of reproductive potential should be advised to use effective contraception during treatment and for at least 3 weeks after the last dose, and males with female partners of reproductive potential should use effective contraception during treatment and for 3 months after the last dose due to potential genotoxicity.

claims.text: Palbociclib is primarily metabolized by CYP3A and the sulfotransferase enzyme SULT2A1, and in vivo it acts as a time-dependent inhibitor of CYP3A; coadministration of a strong CYP3A inducer (rifampin) decreased palbociclib plasma exposure by 85% in healthy subjects. The label advises avoiding concomitant use of strong CYP3A inhibitors (e.g., clarithromycin, itraconazole, ketoconazole, ritonavir) and strong CYP3A inducers (e.g., phenytoin, rifampin, carbamazepine, enzalutamide, St. John's Wort), and to avoid grapefruit or grapefruit juice during treatment; if a strong CYP3A inhibitor cannot be avoided, the IBRANCE dose should be reduced.

claims.text: PALOMA-2 (Phase 3), first-line setting: palbociclib plus letrozole significantly improved progression-free survival versus placebo plus letrozole in postmenopausal women with ER+/HER2- advanced breast cancer, with median PFS of 24.8 months versus 14.5 months (a 10-month improvement), consistent with earlier PALOMA-1 findings.

citations.title: Palbociclib and Letrozole in Advanced Breast Cancer | New England Journal of Medicine
citations.supporting_text: The median progression-free survival of 14.5 months in the placebo–letrozole group in PALOMA-2 is consistent with that observed in other recent studies of letrozole in similar populations... the longer (by 10 months) median progression-free survival with palbociclib–letrozole in PALOMA-2 was consistent with that observed in PALOMA-1. The median progression-free survival of 24.8 months in PALOMA-2 is longer than that seen in other phase 3 studies involving women with advanced breast cancer.

claims.text: In the final overall survival analysis of PALOMA-2 (median follow-up 90 months), median OS was numerically longer with palbociclib plus letrozole (53.9 months) versus placebo plus letrozole (51.2 months), but this difference was not statistically significant (HR 0.956, 95% CI 0.777–1.177).
claims.evidence_type: Clinical trial (Phase 3 final OS analysis, press release corroborated by ASCO Post)

citations.title: Pfizer Announces Overall Survival Results from Phase 3 PALOMA-2 Trial of IBRANCE® (palbociclib)
citations.supporting_text: With a median follow-up of 90 months, patients receiving IBRANCE in combination with letrozole had numerically longer OS compared to placebo plus letrozole (median (95% CI) 53.9 months (49.8–60.8) vs median 51.2 months (43.7–58.9)); the results were not statistically significant (Hazard Ratio (HR)=0.956 [95% CI, 0.777–1.177]).

claims.text: PALOMA-3 (Phase 3), in patients with disease progression after prior endocrine therapy: palbociclib plus fulvestrant significantly improved progression-free survival versus placebo plus fulvestrant, with median PFS of 11.2 months versus 4.6 months (HR 0.50, 95% CI 0.40–0.62; absolute difference 6.6 months).

gaps: Comprehensive dose-reduction schedule tables (starting dose to first/second reduction levels, e.g., 125→100→75 mg) were referenced in the label sections but full table detail was not retrieved verbatim in this search; MSLs should refer to the current full Prescribing Information Section 2.2/2.3 for exact stepwise dose modification tables.

Detailed common non-hematologic adverse events (e.g., fatigue, alopecia, stomatitis, diarrhea, nausea) with exact incidence percentages by trial arm were only partially captured (a partial list appeared in the 2015 label search snippet) and were not confirmed against the most current label; full updated AE tables should be verified directly on DailyMed/FDA before clinical use.

Direct label text for the newer combination indication with inavolisib (approved 2024) and its specific efficacy/safety data (INAVO120 trial results referenced via the Itovebi label) were only tangentially captured; a dedicated review of the current IBRANCE label sections reflecting the inavolisib combination indication is recommended.

No information was found in this search regarding IBRANCE use in men beyond a brief label statement that the safety profile in men is consistent with women; detailed male-specific dosing/monitoring nuances were not located.

Comparative efficacy/safety versus other CDK4/6 inhibitors (ribociclib, abemaciclib) was not directly assessed in this search and any such comparison should be treated as indirect/cross-trial and interpreted cautiously.
Renal impairment dosing guidance was not retrieved in this search; should be confirmed from the current full label (Section 8.6 or equivalent) before clinical counseling.
warnings: Overall survival benefit was NOT statistically significant in either PALOMA-2 (first-line, with letrozole) or PALOMA-3 (post-progression, with fulvestrant) despite significant and clinically meaningful PFS benefits in both trials; this distinction is important for accurate MSL scientific exchange and should not be conflated with a proven survival benefit.

Adverse reaction and pharmacokinetic figures were drawn from multiple label versions/snippets (2015, 2019, 2024, 2025) retrieved via search; because IBRANCE labeling has been updated multiple times (including for new combinations with inavolisib and new HER2+ maintenance indication), the most current full Prescribing Information on DailyMed or FDA should be consulted directly to confirm any figure before clinical or promotional use.

The June 2026 HER2+ maintenance approval (PATINA trial) is a very recent regulatory action; some secondary source (Oncology Nursing News) content appeared to closely track the FDA announcement language, and full FDA-posted prescribing information for this specific indication should be checked on Drugs@FDA once available, as noted by FDA's own statement that full PI would be posted separately.

Search results included tertiary sources (news/nursing sites) alongside primary FDA/DailyMed sources; primary sources were prioritized for label claims, but efficacy commentary from secondary sources was cross-checked against primary trial publications where possible.
